source_title: Targeted rehabilitation may improve patient flow and outcomes: development and implementation of a novel Proactive Rehabilitation Screening (PReS) service
locator: Methods, PReS screening timing; Results, screening time and cohort flow.
source_setting: Adult acute medical/surgical wards at a large Australian tertiary hospital; weekday screen for rehabilitation needs, linked to physician assessment and potential acute in-reach or subacute inpatient rehabilitation.
source_n: 4,000 consecutive screening episodes; acute ward subgroup n=2,949; the article reports n=1,604 screened in the day 5-7 target window.
quantity: Screening achieved in target window (days 5-7 after acute admission) among acute ward admissions
source_evidence_basis: The article states that screening for acute-ward patients was achieved within days 5-7 in 86.9% of cases and gives n=1,604. The methods specify day 5, shifting to the next weekday when it falls on a weekend.
limitations: The reported numerator and percentage do not arithmetically match the stated subgroup denominator (1,604/2,949 is not 86.9%); retain the published values as reported and resolve denominator from the source figure before quantitative calibration. Single Australian site, under-75 cohort; this was a screening service rather than universal multidisciplinary assessment.
inferred_scenario_use: Model screening due dates, weekend deferral, missed-record retry, and referral/physician assessment as separate steps. Treat the reported rate as a workflow signal pending denominator resolution, not a transferable local probability.

source_title: Targeted rehabilitation may improve patient flow and outcomes: development and implementation of a novel Proactive Rehabilitation Screening (PReS) service
locator: Results, screening timing among patients screened after ICU transfer.
source_setting: Same Australian acute hospital PReS service; ICU survivors screened after return to acute ward.
source_n: 1,051 screening episodes after transfer from ICU.
quantity: Median time from hospital admission to screening for patients screened after ICU transfer
source_evidence_basis: The primary article reports a median of nine days from admission to screening for the ICU-transfer subgroup, with an interquartile range of seven to fifteen days.
limitations: Conditional ICU subgroup at one hospital; this is time to a screening episode, not time to full rehabilitation assessment or treatment. Not a US or RWJ estimate.
inferred_scenario_use: Allow ICU transfer and return-to-ward to reset screening eligibility, and distinguish screening delay from clinical assessment, acceptance, and first treatment.

source_title: Targeted rehabilitation may improve patient flow and outcomes: development and implementation of a novel Proactive Rehabilitation Screening (PReS) service
locator: Results and Table 1, screening duration across ten consecutive weekdays.
source_setting: Same Australian acute hospital; rehabilitation nurse performed weekday PReS case finding using medical records.
source_period: Ten consecutive weekdays within the May 2017-February 2019 service period; exact dates not stated in the cited text.
source_n: 158 screening episodes observed across 10 weekdays; 561 total minutes.
quantity: Mean staff time per screening episode
source_evidence_basis: The observed total was 561 minutes for 158 screenings over ten weekdays, reported by the authors as an average of 3.6 minutes per screening.
limitations: This is chart-screening workload, not multidisciplinary bedside assessment or therapy time. Single service, paper records, and only ten observed days; no distribution is reported.
inferred_scenario_use: Keep case-finding labor separate from rehabilitation physician/therapist assessment and treatment resources. Use only as an external screening-workload reference.

source_title: Timing and Intensity of Rehabilitation Services During Acute Stroke Hospitalization: Impacts on Functional Recovery and Community Discharge
locator: Methods, analytic sample and measures; Results, discharge function models (PT full model). Time to evaluation measured in days from admission to initial therapy evaluation.
source_setting: Acute ischemic-stroke hospitalizations across a 13-hospital Colorado health system, including a 678-bed Level I trauma center; OT and PT analyzed separately.
source_n: Final analytic samples: PT n=979 and OT n=713; cohorts overlap because many received both disciplines.
quantity: Adjusted association of each additional day to PT evaluation with discharge mobility function
unit: AM-PAC 6-Clicks mobility score points per additional day
source_evidence_basis: In the fully adjusted PT model, an additional day before the initial PT evaluation was associated with a 0.129-point lower discharge mobility score. The endpoint is acute-care discharge function, not an inpatient rehab-facility outcome.
limitations: Retrospective observational association in acute stroke care; residual confounding and illness severity may influence timing and function. AM-PAC is not the IRF-PAI measure, and effect should not be interpreted causally or transferred as a rehab-hospital coefficient.
inferred_scenario_use: Represent assessment timing and function tracking as separate process and outcome fields; use the association to motivate local sensitivity analysis only, not to forecast a causal benefit from earlier therapy.

source_title: Timing and Intensity of Rehabilitation Services During Acute Stroke Hospitalization: Impacts on Functional Recovery and Community Discharge
locator: Results, Table 1; community discharge and admission/discharge AM-PAC function by OT/PT cohort.
source_setting: Same acute stroke hospital system; patients receiving OT or PT during hospitalization.
source_n: OT cohort n=713; PT cohort n=979; cohorts overlap and are not mutually exclusive.
quantity: Community discharge share and mean function scores at admission and discharge, by therapy cohort
unit: percent; AM-PAC 6-Clicks score (range 6-24; higher indicates greater independence)
source_evidence_basis: The cohort table reports separate community-discharge proportions and admission/discharge function means for OT and PT recipients. These are descriptive outcomes among selected service recipients.
limitations: Acute stroke cohort rather than inpatient rehabilitation facility; OT/PT groups overlap and differ by patient mix. These descriptive comparisons cannot estimate discipline effects or serve as local placement probabilities.
inferred_scenario_use: Track functional status and discharge destination as distinct outcomes and retain discipline-specific denominators. Require local clinical assessment data before estimating destination transitions.

source_title: Association of Functional Status and Discharge Destination for Patients Discharged from Inpatient Rehabilitation
locator: Abstract, national IRF dataset and results; discharge self-care and mobility scores associated with community destination.
source_setting: US Medicare Inpatient Rehabilitation Facilities, national standardized functional assessment data.
source_n: 490,032 IRF patients in the first 12 months of national data collection.
quantity: Adjusted association between one-unit higher discharge function score and odds of community discharge
unit: odds ratio per one score unit; percent range
source_evidence_basis: The abstract reports that higher discharge self-care and mobility scores were associated with community rather than noncommunity destination, using national IRF assessment data. Functionally independent patients commonly went to a community setting.
limitations: Observational association from one historical year of Medicare IRF data; scores and discharge destinations reflect case mix, policy, payer, family support, and facility context. Association is not a causal effect or a placement probability for an individual.
inferred_scenario_use: Include admission/discharge function and placement destination as linked but separate state variables. Use the relation qualitatively or for external comparison, not as a local causal rule.
